detail.title: Contingency in Environmental Remediation Cost Estimation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research is based on committee work for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM).
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive funding from any source; however, NASEM reimbursed travel expenses for attending committee meetings in Richland, Washington, from June 2021 to June 2023 (with most meetings held online).

detail.abstract: Cost estimation for hazardous waste remediation has evolved with the implementation of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (CERCLA). CERCLA requires cost estimates for the remediation of hazardous waste sites, of which there are thousands in the US, including mines and oil wells. Because these costs are uncertain, several federal agencies have issued cost-estimating guidelines that describe how to estimate costs and conduct cost-uncertainty analysis. The largest hazardous waste remediation program in the United States at the Hanford Nuclear Site (Richland, Washington) is managed by the US Department of Energy, Office of Environmental Management (DOE-EM), under the "Tri-Party Agreement" among DOE-EM, the US Environmental Protection Agency, and the Washington State Department of Ecology, initially signed in 1989 and updated in 2025. To account for uncertainty, this paper recommends that environmental remediation cost estimators consider the following factors when estimating contingency: (1) the cost estimate's probability distribution, (2) its standard deviation, (3) the confidence interval that the final cost will fall within the assumed accuracy range, and (4) the risk aversion of stakeholders who pay for or monitor the estimated costs. It concludes that cost contingencies (covering unknown unknowns) for many Hanford projects are reasonably estimated. However, the cost of "Radioactive Liquid Tank Waste Stabilization and Disposition" increased from $54.5 billion in 2017 to $213.9 billion in 2018 and to around $364 billion in 2025, suggesting that many unknown unknowns could remain.

title: The Impact of Regulatory Reforms on Volatility in the Indian Stock Market: An Empirical Analysis Post-2016 Demonetization and GST Implementation

detail.title: The Impact of Regulatory Reforms on Volatility in the Indian Stock Market: An Empirical Analysis Post-2016 Demonetization and GST Implementation
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of major regulatory reforms on volatility patterns in the Indian stock market, with particular focus on the 2016 demonetization policy and the 2017 implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST). Using daily data from the National Stock Exchange (NSE) Nifty 50 and Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) Sensex indices spanning 2015 to 2025, this study employs GARCH family models to analyze volatility dynamics and structural breaks in market behavior. The empirical findings reveal that while demonetization caused immediate short-term volatility spikes-with the Sensex declining 6.12% on the announcement day-the medium-term impact demonstrated reduced volatility and enhanced market stability. The GST implementation showed similar patterns, with initial disruption followed by improved market efficiency and a 21% rally in major indices within the first year post-demonetization. Further analysis of recent SEBI reforms in the derivatives segment (2024-2025), including the elimination of daily options expiries and tripling of contract sizes, indicates a deliberate shift toward reducing speculative trading and protecting retail investors. The study contributes to the literature on emerging market finance by demonstrating that well-intended regulatory interventions, despite causing short-term disruptions, can enhance long-term market stability in developing economies. The findings have significant implications for policymakers in other emerging markets considering similar structural reforms.cleartax+3

detail.abstract: This paper argues that contemporary autonomous production systems introduce an irreversible ontological rupture between value creation and human labor. Unlike previous technological waves, which displaced tasks while preserving human centrality in production, current systems optimize, coordinate, and reproduce value independently of human agency. As a consequence, the wage-labor nexus and employment-based distributive mechanisms cease to function as organizing principles of economic life. The paper reframes the crisis not as one of unemployment or skills mismatch, but as a structural exhaustion of the labor-capital dialectic. It concludes that policy responses anchored in re-employment, re-skilling, or labor activation fail to address the core transformation: the emergence of an economy that no longer requires a biological producer-consumer loop to sustain accumulation.

detail.abstract: We extend the human–AI contracting framework of Bastani and Cachon (2025) by introducing time as an endogenous state variable governing human attention. While prior work shows that motivating vigilance becomes prohibitively expensive as AI reliability increases, we demonstrate that this result reflects a deeper institutional failure: supervision is a time-bearing activity whose cost grows endogenously with prolonged error-free operation. We model attention as a decaying stock and show that even incentive-compatible contracts fail to sustain vigilance over time. The resulting equilibrium features performative supervision, strategic blindness, and a preference for system variance. Our findings reframe human–AI collaboration as a temporal coordination problem rather than a pure incentive design challenge, with implications for AI governance, organizational design, and the economics of observation.

title: Fund Proliferation, Decentralization, and Shareholder Power
affiliations: Boston College - Carroll School of Management, Boston College, Carroll School of Management and University of Toronto - Department of Economics

detail.title: Fund Proliferation, Decentralization, and Shareholder Power
detail.abstract: The asset management industry is increasingly shifting toward tailored portfolios, fund proliferation, and decentralization of stewardship—trends partly driven by growing heterogeneity in investor preferences. While these developments better align investment products with investor demands, they also reshape ownership structures, potentially leading to more fragmented ownership and weaker managerial oversight. We develop a framework to evaluate these trade-offs and show that fund proliferation does not necessarily weaken governance: Stronger incentives for asset managers and concentrated portfolios of specialized funds can offset these effects, especially when investor preferences are intense. However, strong investor preferences can also induce asset managers to compete on a new margin—granting investors control by decentralizing stewardship and adopting pass-through voting—without internalizing the associated governance costs.

title: The Luxury of Rounding: Heuristics and Private Information
affiliations: and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Luxury of Rounding: Heuristics and Private Information
detail.abstract: We study how deviations from commonly used decision heuristics can reveal economically meaningful private information. In our empirical setting of loan amount choices on a major FinTech platform, we show that borrowers' non-rounding behavior predicts credit risk beyond standard observables used in screening and pricing. Using unique field data, a stylized model, and complementary evidence from a natural experiment and a laboratory experiment, we identify a mechanism in which financially constrained borrowers have stronger incentives to incur cognitive costs and choose more precise, non-heuristic amounts. These borrowers subsequently experience systematically worse repayment outcomes, yet this information is not reflected in the platform-set interest rates, exposing retail investors to disproportionate risk. Our findings highlight a general channel through which subtle deviations from heuristics transmit private information and help alleviate information frictions in economic decision-making.

title: Which Accounting Signals Predict Future Value Creation?

detail.title: Which Accounting Signals Predict Future Value Creation?

detail.abstract: This research note examines which accounting characteristics are most informative about future fundamental value creation, rather than future stock returns. Much of the existing literature evaluates predictors of equity returns, which combine changes in operating performance with changes in market pricing. In contrast, this study focuses on the first component alone by forecasting an accounting-based proxy for total shareholder return constructed from earnings changes, dividends, and share issuance. Using financial-statement data parsed from SEC EDGAR filings for 1,212 U.S. firms, I construct a set of features capturing investment behavior, profitability, growth momentum, margin stability, and accounting quality. A gradient-boosting classifier is used to predict the direction of next-period changes in the shareholder-return proxy, and feature importance is evaluated using model-agnostic permutation tests. The results indicate that measures of revenue and earnings momentum, investment consistency, and accruals quality are the most reliable predictors of subsequent improvements in fundamental performance. These findings are robust across alternative model specifications, benchmark classifiers, and subperiods. The analysis does not aim to propose a trading strategy; rather, it provides an empirical characterization of which accounting variables are most closely associated with genuine improvements in firm-level value create.

title: Private Enforcement of the Digital Markets Act: Filling Holes and Creating New Ones in Harmonized Enforcement

detail.title: Private Enforcement of the Digital Markets Act: Filling Holes and Creating New Ones in Harmonized Enforcement

publicationDetails.detailsText: Legal Issues of Digitalization, Robotization and Cyber Security in the Light of EU Law. Kluwer International. pp. 145-161

detail.abstract: The recent decade has witnessed several new elements or innovations in the European Union: partial regulation of damages claims related to harm caused by violation of competition rules, strengthening powers of national competition authorities (NCAs)and a new pro-competition instrument on ex-ante regulation of designated gatekeepers – the Digital Markets Act (DMA). Along these legislative acts, update of block exemptions and the soft law of the European Commission reflect current challenges of the digital economy and functioning of digital markets, as well as sustainability and green transition aspects. The adoption of the DMA was followed by vigorous discussion in academia, on the position of the DMA, its legal basis, its provisions and its relationship with competition law and to ex-ante regulation. These discussions are not surprising because the DMA did not come out of the blue but it is an apparent reaction to previous and pending cases against the BigTech launched under EU or national competition law. The regulation of BigTech became the EU’s existential due to the economic power of the BigTech and the limits of traditional ex-post control by competition law in the dynamic digital markets. The enforcement regime is ‘Commission-centric’ – Art. 16 to 36 DMA provide a comprehensive system of investigation and sanction powers of the European Commission and only “residual” powers to enforce national laws [Art. 38(1) to (3) DMA] and to support the European Commission’s investigation [Art. 38(6) and (7) DMA] are left to NCAs. Moreover, the DMA stresses multiple times that the European Commission is the sole enforcer of the DMA. Thus, the DMA explicitly restricted the manoeuvring space of other measures of public enforcement of the DMA than the European Commission. The research questions for this chapter are focused on the extent of possible private enforcement of the DMA, its limits and challenges, and comparison of the private enforcement of the DMA with private enforcement of the EU competition rules and their possible interplay. For the purposes of this chapter, private enforcement of the DMA will be understood as employment of any measures by private parties against designated gatekeepers in the case of violation on non-compliance of the DMA, enforcement of the DMA by private actors vis-à-vis other private entities, private law consequences of application or violation of the DMA, including claims for damages.

title: Role Dynamics in Student-AI Collaboration: A Heterogeneous Transition Network Analysis Approach
affiliations: University of Eastern Finland, FernUniversitat in Hagen,  and University of Eastern Finland

detail.title: Role Dynamics in Student-AI Collaboration: A Heterogeneous Transition Network Analysis Approach

declarations.funderStatement: This article has been co-funded by the European Commission through the ISILA (2023-1-FI01-KA220-HED-000159757) project and the Research Council of Finland through the project CRETIC (360746).

detail.abstract: In this study, we introduce Heterogeneous Transition Network Analysis (HTNA), a variant of Transition Network Analysis (TNA) that acknowledges different node classes within the same network. We propose this method as an analytical solution to model human-AI collaboration where humans take different intents and AI enacts appropriate roles in response. We exemplify the method in a case study examining the collaborative problemsolving process between students and AI through their dialogic exchanges. Our dataset includes 1,915 student-AI interactions from 95 unique students collected in a programming course which were annotated to capture the students' intents as well as the role assumed by AI in its response. We used HTNA to model the iterative flow of these exchanges and identify recurring typed patterns that characterise how students and the AI respond to one another across multiple steps. The approach captures these higher-order structures while preserving core TNA features such as bootstrapping, and it can be extended with additional measures, including centrality measures, communities and cliques, to further examine the dynamics of human-AI collaboration.

title: Private (Non-)Enforcement of Competition Law in Slovakia

detail.title: Private (Non-)Enforcement of Competition Law in Slovakia

publicationDetails.detailsText: EU and Comparative Law Issues and Challenges Series (ECLIC), 8, 40-69. DOI 10.25234/eclic/35829

detail.abstract: Slovakia transposed the Damages Directive (2014/104) in the simplest way-copying its provision into separate law and repealing previous provisions tackling possibility of the private enforcement of competition law, including collective rights of consumers or their association. The Damages Directive was popularly presented as a "fresh start" for public enforcement of competition law in the EU Member States and to solve some interplays regarding access to file and protection of leniency submissions. Nevertheless, the Damages Directive left several loopholes in private enforcement since it covers merely "some" provisions on damages claims. The paper will investigate level of private claims arising from the violation of competition rules in Slovakia, reasons for such a level and provides some avenues for further incentives to enforce competition rules outside the administrative procedure at the Slovak NCA. First, preliminary observation regarding stand-alone actions can show to us certain unwillingness of Slovak courts to provide a civil remedy in cases of alleged violation of the competition rules. The Supreme Court of the Slovak Republic in the cases involving dispute between a health insurance company and hospitals refused to provide an injunction without prior decision of the competition authority. This decision was based on the argument that courts are bound by the decision of competition authority in terms of administrative offence punished by that authority. Thus, the paper will provide an answer to the question, whether this position of the Supreme Court, in fact, limited the possibility of success of stand-alone actions. Second, from the analysis of the investigation activity of the Slovak NCA, it is apparent that in the recent years it focuses almost purely on investigation of bid rigging cartels. In this context, the paper will assess whether the decision of the competition authority provide enough information for possible follow-on action. Indeed, in bid rigging cases, such assessment will be easier, comparing to abuse of dominance. Nevertheless, the paper will try to estimate possible overall damages caused by anti-competitive behaviour identified by the Slovak NCA. In this context, it must be noted, that in Slovakia, it is better to call enforcement of competition rules through means of civil law "public-private" enforcement rather that "private" enforcement because action can be filed by public authority (or in some cases more precisely the Slovak Republic as state represented by a public authority) harmed by bid rigging, rather than individuals. The paper reviewed the recent decisions of the AMO if they can serve as a basis for follow-on action, based on four criteria: (1) if they are final, (2) if the described behaviour caused a relevant harm, (3) if the injured party contributed intentionally or negligently into infringement, and (4) if it is possible to find a liable person with assets enough to cover damages. The analysis showed that only a small fraction of the decision of the AMO passed through this scrutiny. Finally, the paper suggests non-exhaustive list of suggestions that can improve possibilities of private damages claims in competition matters: the rebuttable presumption that anti-competitive behaviour raised prices by 10 %, involvement of the “victims” as a third parties, including damages consideration in the settlement procedure, solving private-law aspects of competition law enforcement by private-law measures. Although the first suggestion requires the statutory change, the remaining can be achieved also via a new practice of the AMO and contracting authorities. Better involvement of the “victims” of competition infringements is, moreover, consistent with similar policies in criminal proceedings.

title: Artificial intelligence adoption for logistics and producer-price inflation volatility: Evidence from European sectoral data

detail.title: Artificial intelligence adoption for logistics and producer-price inflation volatility: Evidence from European sectoral data
detail.abstract: Using Eurostat AI-in-enterprises data on AI for logistics and monthly producer price indices for 26 EU countries and 16 sectors, we estimate country, sector, and year fixed-effects models. Higher AI adoption in year t predicts lower realized PPI inflation volatility in year t+1 (β = -0.0019, s.e. = 0.0007). A 10 p.p. increase in adoption corresponds to a 0.0002 decline in volatility (about 0.6% of the mean). The energy-volatility interaction indicates state dependence, and a placebo shows no prediction of past volatility.

title:
Information-Driven Volatility as a Measure-Valued Stochastic Process: 
A Probability-Theoretic and Control-Theoretic Framework for Market Dynamics

detail.title:
Information-Driven Volatility as a Measure-Valued Stochastic Process: 
A Probability-Theoretic and Control-Theoretic Framework for Market Dynamics
detail.abstract: We develop a long-form probability-theoretic framework in which market volatility emerges endogenously from information arrival and persistence. Information flow is modeled as a Markov measure-valued stochastic process (µ t) t≥0 on M(R +). Volatility is defined as a stable operator acting on measures, σ(µ) = Σ(g dµ), rather than as an exogenous diffusion. This construction generates volatility clustering via memory in the information measure and unifies diffusion-driven, jump-driven, and self-exciting market event dynamics under a single operatorbased representation. We establish well-posedness and stability of the induced price dynamics, derive no-arbitrage conditions through an equivalent martingale measure via Girsanov, and formulate a measure-valued stochastic control problem with an associated infinite-dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation in viscosity sense. We further show how classical models including Black-Scholes, Heston-type volatility, and Hawkes/self-exciting volatility arise as special cases or reductions. The framework provides a principled bridge between information flow, liquidity, and risk, offering structural explanations for clustered volatility and heavy-tailed returns.

title: Environmental Impacts of China's Overseas Development Projects
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS), Department of Economics and Columbia University

detail.title: Environmental Impacts of China's Overseas Development Projects
detail.abstract: While the economic and social benefits of  foreign aid and development finance receipt are well-established, relatively little is known about  the environmental impacts  in recipient countries. China has undertaken overseas investment projects on a massive scale across more than 140 countries. This paper quantifies their impacts on key ecological outcomes: deforestation, land use, air pollution, and biodiversity. Using 6,303 geocoded Chinese finance projects from 2000-2023 combined with satellite and biodiversity data, we find that project implementation leads to an immediate and persistent decline in surrounding vegetation by 0.3%, equivalent to an average annual loss of 4,755 km2 of vegetated land worldwide. Air quality also deteriorates, with aerosol optical depth rising  0.9%. Biodiversity losses are concentrated among higher trophic groups: bird species richness declines by 1.6% and mammalian richness by 0.1%. Translating vegetation loss into reduced carbon sink capacity implies annual emissions of 52-174 million tons of CO2e, corresponding to annual  global welfare losses of $2.6-$33.1 billion.

title: Does Social Capital Matter in Banking? Evidence from Community Banks
affiliations: Southern Methodist University (SMU) - Finance Department and University of Oklahoma - Michael F. Price College of Business

detail.title: Does Social Capital Matter in Banking? Evidence from Community Banks
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of social capital on banking operations and performance. Using data from 2006 to 2018, we examine how varying levels of social capital across U.S. counties affect different types of banks, finding an impact mostly at community banks. We employ a novel proxy for social capital that exhibits county-year variation: the percentage of tax filings reporting charitable contributions. To address endogeneity concerns and validate the measure, we instrument it with other well-established yet less-varying proxies for social capital-organ donation rates and high voter turnout-showing consistent results throughout. Our findings reveal that community banks in high-charitable contribution counties experience higher deposit growth, are less likely to exit these markets, and show a greater propensity to lend. This favors underserved businesses, including small businesses and minority-or femaleowned enterprises. Conversely, larger banks exhibit opposite or no trends.

title: Adverse Selection and Information Chasing in OTC Markets: Whose Information Matters and Why?
affiliations: BI Norwegian Business School, University of Hamburg and Brandeis University - International Business School

detail.title: Adverse Selection and Information Chasing in OTC Markets: Whose Information Matters and Why?
detail.abstract: This study identifies striking differences between OTC and order-driven markets in the influence of asymmetric information. Using highly detailed data from the world's largest OTC market, the paper first provides evidence that OTC bid-ask spreads are driven by two information asymmetries, rather than one. The paper also provides evidence that OTC dealers adopt three strategic responses to client information, rather than one, with the choice determined by client type: widen spreads, consistent with adverse selection; narrow spreads, consistent with information chasing; and no response, consistent with uninformed clients. Adverse selection is more likely for clients engaged in HFT.

detail.title: Drill Baby Drill: Global Implications of US Fossil Fuel Energy Production and Consumption Revival

publicationDetails.detailsText: Published in Book: The Impact of Carbon Pricing on Green Investment in Manufacturing

detail.abstract: In 2025, President Trump said in his inauguration speech at the US Capitol that we will "drill, baby, drill." This remark was the beginning of the US retreat from the clean energy transition and the revival of US fossil fuel energy production and consumption. This study explores the nature of this development, the potential benefits, criticisms, challenges and the global implications. I show that the drill baby drill executive order has the potential to increase oil and gas production in the US, increase energy independence for the US, create more jobs for Americans, lower energy prices, reduce inflation, and maintain the US global leadership in energy markets. However, several domestic, regional and global risks abound which need to be mitigated.

title: Japan's Smartphone Act (MSCA) in the Shadow of Competition Law Under-Enforcement
affiliations: Kyoto University - Graduate School of Law

detail.title: Japan's Smartphone Act (MSCA) in the Shadow of Competition Law Under-Enforcement
detail.abstract: Following the EU’s Digital Markets Act, Japan has enacted a targeted, sector-specific digital competition rule for the smartphone software ecosystem: the Mobile Software Competition Act (MSCA). While much attention focuses on the MSCA, it should be recalled that the MSCA did not emerge in a vacuum; it was introduced as a legislative response to the persistent ineffectiveness and chronic under-enforcement of Japan’s competition law, the Anti-Monopoly Act (AMA), particularly in abuse cases. Even a workable MSCA is a highly targeted, symptomatic intervention that cannot cure the underlying AMA problem. Against this backdrop, setting the MSCA’s doctrinal details aside, this piece revisits the AMA’s under-enforcement problem, examines its causes, and sketches tentative reform ideas—drawing on a comparison with Korea, a jurisdiction with broadly similar institutional features but markedly different enforcement outcomes. It argues that statutory hurdles, judicial passivity, and the JFTC’s risk-averse enforcement stance may be key underlying causes of the under-enforcement of the AMA, and it offers preliminary policy ideas, including the introduction of statutory presumptions of market power, more strategic enforcement practices (by invoking unfair trading practices and monopolization concurrently), and organizational overlaps in enforcement (by granting AMA enforcement powers to independent bodies other than the Japan Fair Trade Commission) to bolster competition enforcement under the AMA.

title: Multi-Physics Field Coupled Power Load Forecasting for Solar Buildings in Cold Regions Based on KC-AOA Optimized Random Forest

detail.title: Multi-Physics Field Coupled Power Load Forecasting for Solar Buildings in Cold Regions Based on KC-AOA Optimized Random Forest
detail.abstract:
Amidst rural clean heating initiatives and dual-carbon goals, accurate electrical load forecasting is pivotal for optimizing renewable energy heating systems in cold regions. This study focuses on solar buildings in Zhangjiakou, a typical continental monsoon climate area, to address the limitations of traditional single-factor load forecasting models (e.g., poor generalization and weak robustness). A multi-physics field coupled load forecasting framework is proposed, integrating meteorological factors (temperature, wind speed, solar radiation, humidity) and temporal features, with hyperparameters optimized by the Kent Chaotic Mapping and Composite-Cycloid co-driven Archimedes Optimization Algorithm (KC-AOA).
          The research methodology follows a systematic pathway of "Data Preparation - Feature Engineering - Model Construction - Validation & Evaluation". First, 11,900 hours of data (meteorological parameters, electrical load, building attributes) were collected and partitioned into training (8,400 hours) and test (3,500 hours) sets without overlap, with Stratified K-Fold (K=5) cross-validation ensuring seasonal distribution consistency. Second, multi-physics field features were engineered based on building thermal dynamics, including radiation intensity grading, wind-induced infiltration heat loss modeling, and apparent temperature correction. Third, the KC-AOA algorithm was developed to optimize Random Forest (RF) hyperparameters, enhancing global search capability via Kent chaotic initialization and balancing exploration-exploitation through composite cycloid-adjusted MOA.

detail.abstract: Parental labor migration, both rural-urban and international, has been extensively examined in relation to children's education. However, empirical evidence on its impact on learning outcomes remains scarce in low-and lower-middle-income countries, largely due to data limitations. This study examines the association of parental migration on children's foundational learning and psychological well-being in Bangladesh using nationally representative data from MICS6 (2019). Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimates suggest strong positive associations between paternal international migration and children's learning outcomes, weaker or insignificant effects of paternal domestic migration, and potential negative consequences of maternal migration. After applying Inverse Probability Weighting with Regression Adjustment (IPW-RA) to mitigate endogeneity bias, the positive paternal effects disappear, while the negative associations of maternal migration with both educational and psychological outcomes has become clearer and more robust. These findings underscore the importance of distinguishing between paternal and maternal migration when assessing the consequences of migration for child development.

title: Programmable Fairness in Electricity Markets: A Cost-Causation-Consistent Alternative to Marginal Pricing

detail.title: Programmable Fairness in Electricity Markets: A Cost-Causation-Consistent Alternative to Marginal Pricing

declarations.funderStatement: The IOTA Foundation

detail.abstract: Electricity markets increasingly rely on flexibility, priority access, and differentiated reliability to maintain adequacy under decarbonisation. Yet prevailing pricing mechanisms-most notably locational marginal pricing (LMP)still treat electricity as a homogeneous commodity and manage scarcity primarily through prices, producing distributional instability and weak cost causation. We propose a programmable market architecture that separates physical feasibility, scarcity allocation, and cost recovery into explicit computational layers. A Shapley-theoretic Automatic Market Maker (AMM) embeds fairness conditions directly into clearing rather than relying on ex post caps, uplift, or compensation. Using a stylised, stress-tested model of the GB electricity system with network constraints and heterogeneous demand contracts, we present a bottomup household instantiation for transparency and measurement, and compare the AMM to marginal pricing. The AMM reduces cost dispersion, improves alignment between system burden and payments, and bounds scarcity exposure while maintaining revenue adequacy-showing that fairness can be treated as a computable property of market design.

Structured Forgetting at the Edge of Deterministic Physics

detail.title:
Navier-Stokes and the Burden of Memory 
Structured Forgetting at the Edge of Deterministic Physics
detail.abstract: The Navier-Stokes equations sit at the centre of classical physics and engineering, yet they harbour one of the deepest open problems in mathematics. Framed by the Clay Mathematics Institute as a Millennium Prize Problem, the challenge concerns the existence and smoothness of solutions in three dimensions. This paper argues that the difficulty is not merely technical but informational. Beginning from the Poisson-Liouville formulation of classical mechanics, we show that fluid motion inherits an ideal of total memory that becomes untenable at scale. Turbulence emerges where information is generated faster than it can be retained. We propose structured forgetting as the missing conceptual lens through which the Navier-Stokes challenge becomes intelligible and accessible. The equations themselves are not wrong. They remember too much. The paper reframes the Navier-Stokes problem as a boundary between deterministic law and necessary forgetting, with implications for mathematics, physics, and complexity science.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines how popular literature at the turn of the 20th century portrayed Wall Street and the rapidly expanding securities markets. Drawing on dime novels and other widely circulated fiction, it shows how authors depicted finance as a predatory arena dominated by powerful market operators who manipulated stock prices, exploited information asymmetries, and acted outside meaningful legal or moral constraint. These narratives framed Wall Street as a rigged system in which insider trading, market manipulation, and speculative schemes determined outcomes far more than supply and demand. Although such works often misunderstood the actual mechanics of securities markets, they reflected—and helped shape—public anxieties about financial power, corporate capitalism, and the vulnerability of ordinary investors. In these stories, the “wolves” of Wall Street invariably triumph while inexperienced traders, seduced by the addictive promise of quick profits, meet financial ruin. This literature offers a revealing cultural history of how Americans interpreted the rise of modern finance and the perceived dangers of speculation.

detail.abstract: We examine the relationship between climate-related financial policies (CRFPs) and banks' systemic risk. Using a sample of 458 banks in 47 countries over the period 2000-2020, we document that more stringent CRFPs are detrimental to overall financial stability and contribute to increased system-wide distress, where excessive regulatory constraints may impose burdens on banks. Decomposing systemic risk shows that stricter climate-related financial policies raise banklevel volatility but not interbank correlation, indicating that higher systemic risk stems from increased individual bank fragility rather than stronger synchronization. We investigate the banklevel transmission channels through which climate-related financial policies may contribute to higher systemic risk. Tighter policies are associated with slower loan growth, lower profitability, an increase in non-performing loans and compressed net interest margins, as funding costs rise faster than lending rates. At the same time, capital adequacy ratios decline, indicating mounting balance sheet pressures. However, the implementation and ratification of the Paris Agreement, more robust adaptation strategies to cope with climate shocks and a higher incidence of natural disasters and a larger number of people affected by extreme climate events may counteract the amplifying effects of CRFPs on systemic risk. Moreover, banks with stronger environmental, social, and governance (ESG) commitments experience less systemic distress when exposed to green financial policies.

detail.abstract: Decentralization is extensively studied in developed economy and democratic contexts in relation to corruption and governance, often focusing on select countries. However, how and why some decentralization ideas get traction while others fall apart, and how this relates to democratization in closed authoritarian regimes is understudied. During the times of political openings, what we call "regime thawing," authoritarian regimes adopt and adapt democratic institutions. Using pre-registered randomized experiment with a large political elite survey (n=1,407) in Uzbekistan, one of the most consolidated modern authoritarian regimes, we find evidence in support for decentralization over policies but not institutions. Although the bureaucrats lose interest over institutional reforms that come with accountability to citizens (vertical), such as policy design levels, political elites prefer decentralization if this helps them define the deliverables at policy implementation levels (political oversight). We do not find that decentralization policies induce democratic institutional attitudes. We provide novel evidence on how decentralization can happen under authoritarian regimes and help them, while not endangering the regime stability.

detail.abstract: This article examines the liquidity effects of a wealth tax on residential rental real estate. Using data from a real estate corporation, we simulate the effects of a wealth tax on cash flows from the rental operations. The level of detail of the data enables us to conduct analyses at the annual, regional and year of construction level. A comparison with real estate data from other sources supports external validity. The results of the simulation show that the introduction of a wealth tax can significantly reduce the cash flow from rental operations and lead to liquidity problems. On average over all observations, a wealth tax rate of 2% leads to a negative cash flow after all costs. In general, this finding implies that growth-oriented real estate is more affected by a wealth tax in terms of liquidity than rental yield-oriented real estate. Particularly in large cities with high market values but relatively low rents, the liquidity effects can be more than three times as high as in rural or industrial regions – potentially leading to a relative loss of investment attractiveness. As a wealth tax is decoupled from rental income, the tax burden is very sensitive to market developments, including the interest rate environment. As a result, investments in residential rental real estate are exposed to additional uncertainty. This additional tax uncertainty might impair the willingness to invest and should therefore be taken into account in political discussions on the reintroduction of a wealth tax.

detail.abstract: This article examines the evolving relationship between India, Japan, and South Korea within the context of the Indo-Pacific region in the past decade. Moving beyond a historical power asymmetry, the rise of China and a shared commitment to a “Free and Open Indo-Pacific” have fostered a new strategic convergence among these three democracies. This article explores the evolving bases of this partnership, focusing on areas of cooperation, such as maritime security, economic development, and technological innovation. It also acknowledges emerging challenges, including navigating a complex regional order and balancing national interests with collective goals. The analysis aims to capture the long-term trajectory of this trilateral partnership, and its potential to shape regional security and prosperity in the Indo-Pacific.

detail.title: THE REPUBLIC OF KOREA’S FOREIGN POLICY APPROACH: From New Southern Policy to the Indo-Pacific Strategy
detail.abstract: This research paper delves into the ever-changing nature of the Republic of Korea’s (ROK) foreign policy specifically in relation to its transition from the New Southern Policy (NSP) to the Indo-Pacific Strategy. By examining its global interactions, relationships, alliances and challenges, the paper explores how the ROK’s policy decisions have been shaped by the regional and global undercurrents. The study provides an analysis of the ROK’s foreign policy choices from Moon Jae-in’s presidency to Yoon Suk-yeol’s term, assessing their alignment with security priorities, middle power status, aspirations of becoming a “Global Pivotal State”, evolving interests and the global security landscape. From the implementation of the NSP to embracing the Indo-Pacific geostrategic framework this research offers an examination of the ROK’s approach to foreign affairs. Ultimately it highlights how foreign policy reflects a nation’s ability to juggle needs, regional powers and international obligations while demonstrating evolution either through progress or continuity

title: Transition from Hedging to Balancing in Australia’s China Policy: Theoretical and Empirical Explorations
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW)

detail.title: Transition from Hedging to Balancing in Australia’s China Policy: Theoretical and Empirical Explorations
detail.abstract: For almost two decades, Canberra hedged its economic and security bets between China – its most significant economic partner – and the United States – its core security ally – rather successfully, with Australian policymakers announcing that the country would not have to choose between the two great powers and that there are ways to maintain a tight alliance with the US while enhancing friendship and cooperation with China. However, Australia-China relations started to deteriorate in the mid-2010s, with Canberra effectively giving up on hedging by signing in 2021 the AUKUS (Australia-UK-US) security pact and undertaking other steps that have been widely received as unequivocally joining the US’s effort to contain China. This article explores Australia’s foreign policy transformation by conceptualising it as a transition from hedging to balancing against China. It develops a theoretical argument about why an essential middle power might decide to give up on hedging and start balancing. It argues that the end of hedging in Australia’s China policy is a result of disappearing structural uncertainty and systemic permissiveness on which hedging, as a pattern of smaller power behaviour, is premised. As such, the article contributes to the knowledge about hedging by highlighting the limitations of smaller power hedging.

detail.abstract: We examine how accounting quality attributes jointly mitigate underpricing across two dimensions of information risk in seasoned equity offerings (SEOs). Using institutional ownership to distinguish settings, we find that accounting comparability mitigates underpricing associated with lower quality accruals in information environments with more potent information asymmetry (substitutive interaction). In less asymmetry-potent settings, we observe higher quality accruals potentiating the effectiveness of comparability in mitigating uncertainty-driven underpricing (complementary gating interaction). The paper informs standard-setter conceptualizations of accounting attributes and advances research on the role of accounting quality in mitigating information risk-related market frictions.

detail.title: Fostering Undergraduate Economics Research with Student-led Journals
detail.abstract: This paper documents the design and implementation of the CWRU Journal of Economics and the TTU Journal for Societal Impact. The two journals offer multiple perspectives on how to develop student-led research initiatives that expand undergraduate research opportunities in economics departments with limited faculty capacity. The journals' key design features-tiered engagement, peer mentorship, and student ownership-are anchored in experiential, situated, and scaffolded learning theories. The project analyzes the impact of the CWRU Journal of Economics' three-layer structure that aligns research tasks with students' evolving skills. Over four semesters, 83 students participated, with survey data showing that those involved for multiple semesters reported significantly higher gains in research ability, data analysis skills, and professional development outcomes, including internships and conference presentations. The initiative has since expanded to include high school outreach, inter-institutional submissions, and media partnerships. This paper offers a replicable model for departments seeking to create scalable, high-impact undergraduate research experiences within resource-constrained environments.

title: Unemployment and Output in India: An Examination of Okun's Law

detail.title: Unemployment and Output in India: An Examination of Okun's Law
detail.abstract: This study discusses the importance of Okun's law in India by examining the relationship between unemployment and output across various states from 1993 to 2011. A panel data framework using fixed and random effects models is applied on state-level data collected from the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) and the Central Statistical Office (CSO). The unit root tests and robustness checks, such as the Hausman test and the use of heteroskedasticityconsistent errors, validate the dependability of the findings. The estimated Okun coefficient of-0.12 indicates that a 1% increase in GDP results in a mere 0.12% reduction in unemployment, which is significantly lower than what is observed in advanced economies. This weak relationship highlights India's phenomenon of jobless growth, influenced by structural rigidities, the prevalence of informal employment, and skill mismatches throughout the study period. The findings suggest that economic growth by itself does not guarantee widespread employment, underscoring the necessity for additional policies like promoting labour-intensive industries, aiding small businesses, and enhancing workforce skills.

detail.abstract: Recent disruptions—including the COVID-19 pandemic, the US–China trade war, and logistical bottlenecks—have fueled widespread claims that global supply chains in Asia are undergoing a fundamental reconfiguration away from China. Focusing on the electronics and machinery sector, the largest component of global trade by value, this article critically examines whether such diversification has materially altered Asia’s production networks. Using trade statistics and firm-level case studies of major companies (Apple, Samsung Electronics, BBK Electronics, and Acer), the analysis shows that supply chain shifts away from China are modest and often overstated. While some labor-intensive final assembly has relocated to Southeast Asia—particularly Vietnam—China remains deeply embedded in intermediate goods production and higher-value manufacturing. Firm strategies largely reinforce the established “Smile Curve” of global value chains: advanced economies dominate R&D and high-value activities, China anchors large-scale manufacturing, and Southeast Asian economies capture lower-value assembly. Country positions along the value chain have remained remarkably stable over the past two decades, despite recent shocks. The findings suggest that, absent major exogenous disruptions, China’s role as the core manufacturing hub for consumer electronics is likely to persist, and that current diversification trends represent incremental adjustment rather than structural transformation of Asian supply chains.

detail.abstract: This study presents the conceptual design, visualization, and physical prototyping of a futuristic unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), titled White Eagle MAR UAV FX15, developed through an iterative process combining hand-drawn sketches, digital rendering, and high-fidelity 3D printing. The prototype is designed to explore advanced aerodynamic shaping, modular structural architecture, and aesthetic-functional integration within next-generation UAV platforms. Starting from an initial conceptual drawing, the UAV geometry was progressively refined into a realistic digital model, preserving the original proportions while introducing practical design elements such as a streamlined fuselage, blended wing-body configuration, integrated sensor housings, and retractable landing gear. The final form emphasizes low-drag aerodynamics, structural symmetry, and surface continuity, aiming to support high-altitude, long-endurance, and carrier-capable operational concepts. The finalized design was materialized as a high-resolution 3D-printed prototype mounted on a solid display base with integrated blue LED illumination. This physical realization enables detailed inspection of geometric accuracy, surface quality, component integration, and visual balance, serving as a bridge between conceptual design and engineering development. The prototype demonstrates how additive manufacturing can be effectively used as a rapid prototyping tool for aerospace design exploration, facilitating early-stage validation, communication, and refinement. Overall, this work illustrates a multidisciplinary workflow that merges creative conceptualization with technical visualization and physical prototyping, offering a scalable framework for future UAV research, design communication, and innovation in aerospace systems.

title: Machines Rising Slowly: Robot Adoption Hasn’t Kicked into High Gear…Yet

detail.title: Machines Rising Slowly: Robot Adoption Hasn’t Kicked into High Gear…Yet

detail.abstract: Despite long-standing fears that automation will rapidly displace human labor, industrial robot adoption has advanced more gradually and unevenly than widely anticipated. This paper examines the pace and determinants of robot diffusion across countries and industries, showing that recent growth in installations largely reflects a low-base effect rather than a structural acceleration in automation. Using cross-country and sectoral evidence, the analysis identifies three key drivers of robot adoption: wage levels and demographic pressures, industrial composition, and the policy and institutional environment. Robots remain concentrated in manufacturing processes dominated by routine, repetitive tasks—most notably in the automotive and electronics sectors—while the technical limits of automation constrain broader diffusion. Comparative case studies of Japan, Germany, South Korea, the United States, and China illustrate how demographics, labor institutions, and adjustment mechanisms shape both adoption rates and labor market outcomes. In particular, strong labor market coordination and reskilling frameworks can mitigate employment losses even amid extensive automation. The paper argues that China represents the pivotal case for the future of global robotization, combining rapid demographic aging, large-scale manufacturing, and proactive industrial policy. Yet even in China, structural and institutional constraints suggest a gradual rather than disruptive transition, implying that robots are arriving more slowly than alarmist narratives suggest—and, paradoxically, perhaps more slowly than China’s productivity challenges require.

detail.abstract: How does local fiscal architecture shape citizen responses to natural hazards? Using survey data from 1,180 respondents across 82 Philippine municipalities merged with typhoon exposure records and administrative fiscal data, we find that municipal liquidity (months of operating expenses in cash reserves) moderates the negative association between hazard intensity and trust. In high-liquidity municipalities, disaster intensity shows no significant relationship with interpersonal or institutional trust. Transfer dependency is associated with increased civic mobilization. Municipalities combining high liquidity with competitive elections exhibit reduced contentious action alongside increased associational engagement. These findings advance understanding of how fiscal institutions structure post-disaster citizenship.

detail.abstract: PURPOSE: This article discusses how the entrepreneurial context influences psychological contracts. It highlights the differences between employment agreements in entrepreneurial settings and those in traditional bureaucratic organizations. DESIGN: We extend psychological contract theory by incorporating the role of salience and illustrating how the risk and uncertainty of entrepreneurial settings influences the formation of psychological contracts and results in psychological contracts which vary significantly in structure and content from those in stable, bureaucratic settings. INSIGHTS: We show that psychological contracts in the entrepreneurial context differ in the types of content or currency exchanged, the forms of agreement between the two parties involved, and the impact of contract breach and violation. Our insights are summarized in a set of testable propositions. RESEARCH LIMITATIONS: The conceptual nature of this study suggests the need for empirical research to validate and expand upon these findings, especially in diverse entrepreneurial contexts. PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS: The insights provided are crucial for entrepreneurs in managing teams, retaining talent and navigating complex investor relationships. This understanding can aid in the transition of businesses from startups to larger organizations. SOCIAL IMPLICATIONS: This research enhances our comprehension of employment dynamics in entrepreneurial settings, offering a foundation for future investigations into the evolving landscape of entrepreneurship, particularly in the context of personalized employment arrangements and team dynamics. ORIGINALITY / VALUE: This research represents a meaningful step in understanding psychological contracts within under-researched entrepreneurial settings, such as small firms and startups. We contribute by expanding the psychological contract literature previously focused on larger organizations.

This essay critically examines the increasing use of the final offer arbitration (FOA) procedure in resolving tax treaty-related disputes in international and EU tax law. It explores the comparative experiences outlined by article 25(5) of the OECD Model, the OECD MLI (Part VI) and the EU Directive No. 1852/2017 (EU DRD), highlighting both advantages and challenges of the FOA model. The analysis focuses on whether an arbitration panel can be recognized as a referral body under article 267 of the TFEU, especially when questions of EU law interpretation arise, referencing the Achmea judgment by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). The essay also evaluates the CJEU's potential interpretative role regarding the EU DRD when national courts of EU Member States submit preliminary rulings. Finally, it considers the position and participatory rights of taxpayers within the arbitration process, noting that the EU DRD, as EU secondary law, must uphold the principles and procedural guarantees enshrined in the European Charter of Fundamental Rights.

detail.abstract: Online health communities (OHCs) have gained increasing attention in chronic disease management (CDM). Existing literature on this topic, however, is mostly based on forum-based OHCs that examine core behavioral mechanisms such as social support, social comparison, or self-monitoring separately. This study introduces a novel chat-based OHC model that jointly captures and quantifies these mechanisms through real-time group interactions and structured behavioral tracking. We draw on real-world data from over 60,000 users and quantify four types of social support (informational, emotional, instrumental, appraisal), three types of social comparison (upward, lateral, downward), and three types of self-monitoring (health indicator check-ins, meal logging, health education) across a 21-day intervention and one-year follow-up, and use hierarchical mixed-effects models to evaluate their effects on obesity, hypertension, and diabetes. We find that all four types of social support are positively associated with weight loss, with informational support showing the largest association. Only downward comparison is significantly associated with better outcomes, suggesting that realistic and achievable benchmarks are more motivating than aiming for much higher or similar standards. The effectiveness of self-monitoring is disease-specific: health indicator check-ins and meal logging are most effective for weight loss, while health education is essential for hypertension and diabetes. Mid-sized groups (around 100 users), higher speaking rates, and lower dropout rates are associated with better outcomes, highlighting the importance and potential of platform design. These insights can effectively guide the development of digital health interventions and chat-based OHC platforms.

detail.abstract:
Periods of apparent stability often precede major systemic disruption. In complex socio-technical environments, risk rarely accumulates in isolation; it forms through interacting pressures that remain partially invisible until decision space has already narrowed. This paper examines how artificial intelligence, climate instability, and geopolitical dynamics increasingly converge to create conditions of deceptive calm, where traditional indicators fail to signal mounting vulnerability.

Rather than offering prediction or prescriptive guidance, the analysis focuses on early-stage recognition: how institutional attention, governance frameworks, and decision latency contribute to delayed response under conditions of accelerating complexity. The paper introduces a convergence-based perspective for understanding how seemingly independent risk domains reinforce one another, and why perception often fails before systems visibly destabilise.

The aim is to support earlier orientation in environments where consequence emerges quietly, long before disruption becomes explicit.

title: Transparency and Accountability in Government Expenditure
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Transparency and Accountability in Government Expenditure
detail.abstract: Persistent challenges of opacity and weak accountability continue to undermine government expenditure management, particularly in developing and emerging economies, where fiscal leakages, inefficiencies, and public distrust remain prevalent. Existing scholarship highlights transparency as a critical prerequisite for improving public financial governance, yet its effectiveness in delivering tangible accountability outcomes remains contested. This study conducts a critical synthesis of empirical and conceptual literature to examine how transparency and accountability mechanisms influence government expenditure efficiency, public trust, and fiscal discipline. Drawing on prior studies, the review analyses the roles of audit trails, fiscal transparency frameworks, and public disclosure mechanisms in shaping expenditure outcomes across different institutional contexts. The findings indicate that enhanced transparency is generally associated with improved expenditure efficiency, stronger compliance with budgetary rules, and increased citizen confidence in public institutions. However, these effects are highly contingent on institutional capacity, political commitment, and the strength of enforcement mechanisms. An important insight emerging from the review is that high levels of formal transparency do not necessarily translate into effective accountability where political incentives are misaligned, and sanctions for noncompliance are weak. The study concludes that transparency alone is insufficient; it must be embedded within robust, enforceable accountability systems to meaningfully improve government expenditure outcomes and ensure sustainable fiscal governance.

detail.abstract: In May 2024, U.S. equity markets transitioned from a T+2 to a T+1 settlement cycle with the goal of reducing counterparty exposure, improving operational efficiency, and lowering settlement fails. This paper evaluates whether equity settlement fails declined following the transition. Using SEC weekly fails-to-deliver data and controlling for proxies of market activity (SPY volume) and volatility (VIX), I implement a natural experiment design comparing pre and post transition periods. Results show that settlement fails increased significantly, by approximately 42 percent, after T+1. Regression analysis confirms that higher fail levels cannot be explained by market activity or volatility alone. A variance equality test shows no strong evidence of a volatility shift, implying the increase represents a structural level change rather than random noise. Visual inspection of regression residuals shows no meaningful heteroskedasticity patterns. I discuss operational implications and directions for future research.

title: Defining the Resilience Frontier: Stackelberg Bi-Level Optimization for Green Humanitarian Logistics

detail.title: Defining the Resilience Frontier: Stackelberg Bi-Level Optimization for Green Humanitarian Logistics
detail.abstract:
The escalating frequency of high-impact disasters, exemplified by the 2023 Türkiye-
Syria earthquakes which resulted in over 50,000 fatalities, necessitates humanitarian logistics
frameworks that simultaneously address rapid deployment, operational sustainability, and
structural resilience. Traditional models often abstract away coordination frictions between public authorities and private providers or evaluate resilience through smooth performance
metrics that fail to capture the discontinuous reality of systemic collapse.
We introduce the Green Emergency Facility Location-Routing Problem (GEFLRP) via a
bi-level multi-objective programming model. The interaction is conceptualized as a Stackelberg
game grounded in Yue and You (2014, 2017): governmental authorities act as the strategic
Leader selecting distribution center locations, while logistics contractors serve as the operational
Follower optimizing vehicle routes to minimize total vehicle-kilometers—a methodology
validated here as a tractable proxy for carbon emissions. By operationalizing Viability Theory,
the model mathematically defines the Resilience Frontier—a deterministic boundary separating
viable "survival zones" from systemic collapse—and links these thresholds to the deprivation
cost framework of Holguín-Veras et al. (2013, 2016).
Using 20 benchmark instances with Taguchi-tuned operator parameters under production
settings (population = 100, iterations = 500) and nested GA/ICA meta-heuristics, this study
quantifies network viability under parametric stress. Comprehensive benchmarking across 400
experimental runs (N = 200 per algorithm) validates the Genetic Algorithm as the preferred
solver: GA achieves 36% faster convergence (1.22s vs. 1.91s, p < 0.001) with 38% lower
standard deviation (σ = 0.37s vs. σ = 0.60s), ensuring computational tractability for iterative
sensitivity analysis. Both algorithms achieve statistically equivalent solution quality (p = 0.977),
confirming that GA's speed advantage does not compromise optimization effectiveness.
The findings reveal discontinuous phase transitions where network collapse occurs
abruptly once fleet resources become the binding constraint. Across 20 benchmark instances, the
Resilience Frontier exhibits heterogeneity: demand frontier median +50% (IQR +50% to +60%;
universal feasibility through +30%), capacity frontier median −60% (IQR −60% to −50%;
universal feasibility through −30%), and temporal frontier 8 hours (collapse at 4 hours). The 64-
hour gap between the 72-hour golden window and the 8-hour frontier demonstrates that vehicle
availability—not time—is the critical vulnerability.

detail.abstract: This study examines the dual reality of Yemen's education system following a decade of protracted conflict: its profound systemic collapse and the emergent, grassroots potential within it to serve as a catalyst for Peacebuilding and gender equality (World Bank, 2023; ECW, 2023). Employing a qualitative, comparative case study design grounded in political economy and feminist analysis, this research synthesizes data from international reports, peerreviewed scholarship (particularly by Yemeni researchers), and documented local initiatives. The findings reveal a landscape where institutional destruction, teacher precarity, and gendered exclusion are pervasive (UNESCO & UNICEF, 2023). However, within this landscape, community-based schools, women-led educational projects, and adaptive learning models demonstrate tangible, though fragmented, potential to foster social cohesion and advance women's agency (Al-Ammar, 2023; Bamakhramah & Al-Sorori, 2022). The analysis incorporates a forward-looking scenario model, projecting trajectories under conditions of stagnation, fragmentation, or managed stability. It concludes that leveraging this potential requires a fundamental paradigm shift-from treating education as a short-term humanitarian service to investing in it as a long-term, strategic pillar of inclusive Peacebuilding (Novelli & Higgins, 2022). This entails context-specific, politically-informed support for locally-owned initiatives, curriculum reform, and guaranteed support for teachers, with a sustained commitment to gender-transformative practices (Kirk & O'Farrell, 2023).

publicationDetails.detailsText: The University of Auckland Business School Research Paper(forthcoming)

detail.abstract:
Tourism is a critical industry in New Zealand, especially where the natural environment and local culture are attractions. Māori, along with their traditions and practices, have long been part of the promotion of Aotearoa (Love & Hall, 2022). Today, Māori collectives offer tourist experiences, such as cultural performances, hāngī meals, and ecotours that highlight the importance of kaitiakitanga (guardianship) of the natural world. Yet, in 2022, the National Iwi Chairs Forum sent an open letter to the government about rāhui being disrespected and ignored over sites of significance, waterways, land, and forest. The Forum commented, “It is one thing to call on Māori to participate in the ancient rituals of karakia to bless events and sites and quite another to ignore and at times support ignoring the ancient rituals of rāhui” (National Iwi Chairs Forum, 2022). 

Indigenous prohibitions have drawn attention from sustainability researchers who have found them to be effective in environmental management (Bambridge, 2016; Fabre et al., 2021; van Halderen, 2020). Indeed, some types of rāhui are recognised in New Zealand legislation, such as the Fisheries Act 1996 and the Conservation Act 1987. Nevertheless, rāhui remain understudied in marketing and tourism; their effect on visitor experiences, consumer behaviour, and purchase intent represents a gap in the literature. Exploring this can help lift the visibility and recognition of rāhui, especially within marketing and tourism. In turn, this will support greater consideration and influence of environmentally and culturally safe practices. 

Historically, much of the writing on rāhui was from pakeha writers seeing through ‘imperial eyes’ (Smith, 2022). Hall (2019) explains this view as determined to characterise and classify into categories, with criteria and ranking. In contrast, the Māori world view is less mechanistic; it is tied to whakapapa—genealogy—that connects people as direct descendants of the land itself (Marsden & Royal, 2003; Mead, 2016). Land, water, and natural resources are living elements that possess wairua or mauri (Henare, 2001). 

The proposed methodology recognises the context from which rāhui descends. It looks to understand rāhui through its whakapapa; its ancestry in the sacred, its relationship to the concept of tapu, its branches and offspring, along with its modern-day faces. This paradigm offers a framework for protocol and kaupapa Māori considerations in gathering, protecting and sharing research findings. Iterative cycles of data collection and theoretical sampling will sit within the kaupapa of whakapapa for the empirical research. Hui focus group discussions with iwi and hapū will set the foundation and mandate for the data collection. The focus will first be on inviting Māori voices on rāhui and how they would like this to be understood before interviewing visitors. 

Understanding how rāhui and other practices shape consumption will provide insights to support the tourism sector, including indigenous-led operators. It will also enrich broader marketing theory, allowing us to draw on long-earned wisdom around sacred scarcity to ensure a bountiful future for the following generations

title: Market Making and Transient Impact in Spot FX

detail.title: Market Making and Transient Impact in Spot FX
detail.abstract: Dealers in foreign exchange markets provide bid and ask prices to their clients at which they are happy to buy and sell, respectively. To manage risk, dealers can skew their quotes and hedge in the interbank market. Hedging offers certainty but comes with transaction costs and market impact. Optimal market making with execution has previously been addressed within the Almgren-Chriss market impact model, which includes instantaneous and permanent components. However, there is overwhelming empirical evidence of the transient nature of market impact, with instantaneous and permanent impacts arising as the two limiting cases. In this note, we consider an intermediate scenario and study the interplay between risk management and impact resilience.

detail.abstract: As Vietnam rapidly integrates into global value chains through agreements like the CPTPP and EVFTA, the primary barriers to economic efficiency are shifting from tariffs to institutional frictions. This paper analyzes the role of institutional quality-specifically legal certainty and contract enforcement-as a determinant of transaction costs in Vietnam's digital supply chain sector. Drawing on New Institutional Economics (NIE) and Transaction Cost Theory, we argue that ambiguity in digital governance frameworks acts as an implicit "tax" on trade. While the Law on Electronic Transactions (2023) provides a statutory foundation for the digital economy, implementation lags and "verification anxiety" continue to drive asset specificity risks for foreign investors. We propose a theoretical model where "Legal Tech" adoption-specifically the integration of the VNeID national identity database-serves as an economic accelerator by reducing information asymmetry. The findings suggest that for emerging economies, investing in "soft infrastructure" (legal governance) yields higher marginal returns than physical infrastructure alone. The pipes are clogged not by silt, but by paperwork.

detail.abstract: This study introduces the Islamic Ḥiwār Framework (IHF), a multi-layered, KPI-based architecture developed to operationalize intra-faith dialogue within Islamic contexts by translating theological, ethical, and institutional principles into measurable performance indicators. Drawing from Islamic epistemology, dialogical ethics, and governance structures, the IHF addresses the need for a strategic, accountable, and scalable model for religious rapprochement. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining expert-based Delphi analysis, AHP-weighted indicator validation, and qualitative document review of intra-Islamic unity initiatives. The research identified 14 strategic domains and 280 KPIs distributed across educational, institutional, digital, jurisprudential, ethical, and governance axes. Key findings highlight the role of dialogical trust, ethical literacy, governance transparency, and AI-enabled feedback systems in sustaining meaningful rapprochement. The study recommends the adoption of IHF metrics by religious councils, seminaries, and ministries to support transparent, performance-oriented dialogue governance. Theoretically, the model bridges classical ijtihād with contemporary strategic frameworks such as Balanced Scorecard and digital maturity indices. Practically, it enables real-time monitoring, stakeholder engagement, and strategic planning aligned with maqāṣid-based institutional objectives. This research offers an original KPI-based contribution to Islamic studies, religious diplomacy, and civilizational strategy.

title: Blockchain for Financial Regulatory Compliance and Corporate Governance Frameworks

detail.title: Blockchain for Financial Regulatory Compliance and Corporate Governance Frameworks
detail.abstract: This article examines the potential of blockchain-based regulatory technology (RegTech) as a tool to address rising regulatory compliance costs and governance challenges in the post-2008 financial landscape. It analyses how blockchain’s core features—decentralization, immutability, cryptographic security and smart contracts—can enhance financial regulatory compliance, embedded supervision, accounting, and know-your-customer (KYC) processes while reducing reliance on intermediaries. The discussion further extends to corporate governance, focusing on blockchain’s capacity to mitigate agency problems between shareholders and directors, including through decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs). While highlighting significant efficiency and transparency gains, the article also critically evaluates the legal, operational and security risks associated with blockchain adoption, concluding that effective regulatory calibration is essential to balance innovation with systemic stability.

detail.abstract: Financial exclusion remains a persistent problem under profit-driven financial capitalism, particularly in developing economies where high costs, strict eligibility requirements, and structural barriers limit access to financial services. This article examines the potential of blockchain-based financial technology (FinTech) to promote financial inclusion within the framework of Social and Solidarity Finance (SSF). It argues that blockchain’s features notably those of decentralization, disintermediation, and automated trust can enhance accessibility, suitability, and affordability of financial services. Through analysis of applications such as mobile banking, digital identity, microfinance, crowdfunding, remittances, and central bank digital currencies, the article demonstrates how blockchain can address systemic weaknesses of conventional finance and support inclusive and sustainable financial development.

detail.abstract: A key element to a company's success is its ability to match its supply to uncertain demand by utilizing different types of capacity contracts. We consider the design of a multi-product supply chain, for which each product requires one or more process capabilities and each process can get capacity from multiple resources. We present a single-period model to determine the capacity investments for these resources in the presence of demand uncertainty and option contracts. (We have also extended the model to a multi-period setting in a companion paper) We derive closed-form solutions to two important special cases of the problem and draw managerial insights about the optimal capacity planning strategy. We then develop a stochastic linear programming algorithm to solve the general single period problem and show that our algorithm outperforms alternative algorithms by means of an empirical study. Finally, with the model and algorithm, we study the effects of common processes and option contracts on capacity planning.

detail.title: Queues With Correlated Inter-Arrival and Service Times
detail.abstract: We study a type of correlated queue in which its inter-arrival and service times are correlated, with their joint distribution being characterized by a copula function. This characterization allows for very generally correlated inter-arrival and service times. For such a queue, we first derive an infinite system of linear equations for the moments of the waiting time, based on which we design an algorithm to calculate the moments of the waiting time. In contrast with traditional methods, our algorithm incorporates a recursive procedure which is computationally much more efficient. Furthermore, we show how the moments and covariances of the inter-departure times of the queue can be obtained based on the moments of the waiting time. Numerical experiments are provided to validate our method.

detail.title: Queues with Auto-Correlated Service Times
detail.abstract: We investigate a first-come-first-served G/G/1 queueing system with autocorrelated service times, a feature prevalent in numerous applications. The service times are modeled as a strictly stationary Markov process, encompassing models such as Markov-modulated, copula-correlated, and autoregressive models as special cases. Analyzing queues with autocorrelated service times is inherently challenging. To address this, we employ the MacLaurin Series Expansion (MSE) method, first introduced in Gong and Hu (1992) and inspired by Smooth Perturbation Analysis (SPA) for computing high-order derivatives. This study further validates the MSE method's applicability and underscores the broader utility of Perturbation Analysis (PA) techniques.

title: Security Analysis of Browser’s Hardware API
affiliations: University of Bahrain

detail.title: Security Analysis of Browser’s Hardware API
detail.abstract:
Hardware APIs are interfaces that access various computer resources, such as USB and Bluetooth. They are recently introduced to web browsers. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that analyse them focusing on their permissions, supported schemes, and policies as no academic studies have examined them from a security perspective.
     We started by analysing its architecture and reviewing its source code. Then, we defined a threat model for them and considered several testing techniques. As a result, we discovered two security vulnerabilities in hardware APIs that affect Chromium browsers, including the most popular browser Google Chrome. First, we discovered an origin spoofing issue in the hardware API permission request. The vulnerability allows adversaries to display a target origin (not owned by the adversary) when requesting permission to access a hardware device. Secondly, we demonstrate a vulnerability in the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) for hardware APIs. The vulnerability allows documents loaded over the file: URI scheme to obtain any hardware API permissions previously granted to other documents under the same scheme. We have reported both issues to Google and obtained a CVE-2022-0803 for the first issue.
   Based on these findings, and to aid in future security research in this area, we developed an inspection tool named WebUSB Inspector. The tool is a Chromium extension dedicated to analysing the security of WebUSB and its applications. It monitors all WebUSB traffic to permitted, accessed hardware by overriding its methods to allow for inspection. We evaluated the tool to ensure it could detect both of the reported issues. In addition, we measured its runtime, which achieved around 1 second per method’s invocation.
